description: Syntax, types, and the main method — your first Java program.

screens.body:
Java is a compiled language: your code gets translated into bytecode, and the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) runs that bytecode on any computer. That's the famous 'write once, run anywhere' promise — the same program runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux.

It's also statically typed, which means every variable declares its type up front. The compiler catches type mistakes before your program ever runs — annoying at first, genuinely helpful forever.

If you know JavaScript, Java will feel like its stricter older sibling: curly braces and semicolons everywhere, but the compiler holds your hand.
screens.heading: Java in one minute
screens.keyPoint: Java compiles to bytecode and runs on the JVM — typed, strict, portable.

screens.body:
Every Java program starts in exactly one place: a method called main. When you run your program, the JVM looks for it and starts executing there.

It always looks like this: public static void main(String[] args). The words are scary but the idea is simple — 'public' means anyone can call it, 'static' means it belongs to the class, 'void' means it returns nothing, and String[] args lets the command line pass in arguments.

You don't need to memorize what each word does yet. Just know: no main method, no program.

screens.heading: The main method — Java's front door

screens.body:
In JavaScript you write let age = 19 and the variable figures out its type. In Java, YOU declare the type: int age = 19. The type is a name tag the variable wears forever — you can't later stuff a String into an int.

The everyday types: int for whole numbers, double for decimals, boolean for true/false, char for a single character (in single quotes), and String — capital S — for text.

The payoff: the compiler yells at you the moment types don't line up, instead of your program silently doing something weird at 2 AM.

screens.body:
Java's version of console.log is System.out.println. It prints whatever you give it, then moves to a new line. System.out.print (no 'ln') prints without the new line.

You can glue values together with +: System.out.println("Age: " + age) prints Age: 19. Mixing text and numbers with + always produces text.

You'll use println constantly for debugging — print the variable, see the value, repeat. Same habit as console.log, slightly longer name.

check.question: Which one prints AND moves to a new line?

screens.heading: Saying things out loud

screens.body:
Good news: Java's if, for, and while look almost identical to JavaScript's. The big differences are the types on loop counters and the mandatory semicolons.

A for loop: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++). Notice int before i — the counter needs its type declared, just like any variable.

Semicolons end every statement. Forget one and the compiler refuses to compile — which is honestly better than JS silently guessing what you meant.

screens.heading: Ifs and loops look familiar
screens.keyPoint: Same loops as JS — plus types and semicolons.

screens.body:
A Java array is a row of boxes that all hold the same type — and the number of boxes is decided when you create it. int[] scores = new int[3] makes exactly 3 slots. You can't add a fourth later.

Fill it at creation with curly braces: int[] scores = {88, 92, 77}. Indexing starts at 0, just like JavaScript.

To ask how many slots: scores.length — no parentheses, it's a property, not a method. (ArrayList, which you'll meet soon, uses the method size() instead.)

screens.body:
JavaScript functions become Java methods, and they wear name tags too: the return type comes first. public static int add(int a, int b) returns an int and takes two int parameters.

void means 'returns nothing' — like a function that just prints. If you promise a return type, every path through the method must return a value of that type.

The static keyword (for now) just means 'call me on the class, not on an object.' You'll meet instance methods — called on objects — in the OOP lesson.
